title: The Athlete Is Becoming a Media Platform. Who Owns the Fan?
html:
Every media-rights negotiation in professional sport rests on an assumption so old that nobody says it out loud any more: that the league controls access to the fan, and therefore the league can sell it.

For four decades that was simply true. If you wanted the game, you went where the game was broadcast. The rights holder owned the pipe, the league owned the content, and the fan was whoever happened to be standing at the other end. It was one of the great business models of the twentieth century, and it worked precisely because there was no alternative route to the audience.

There is now. It runs through the athlete.

The uncomfortable arithmetic

Streaming platforms are projected to spend around $14.2 billion on sports rights in 2026, up roughly 7% on 2025. That number gets read as strength, and in the short term it is. But look at what it buys: a fixed term, a defined set of windows, and a licence to distribute. It does not buy a relationship. When the term ends, the rights holder has an expired contract and the league has to sell the same thing again.

Meanwhile, athlete-hosted shows — the Kelce brothers, Draymond Green, Angel Reese among them — command audiences in the millions and attract seven-figure sponsorship on their own account. Those audiences did not come from a rights deal, are not licensed from anyone, and do not expire. eMarketer's framing is the one worth sitting with: an athlete running their own channel functions less like a spokesperson and more like a media property, with its own distribution that marketers cannot fully script or own.

Note what that sentence implies for the league as well as the marketer.

Distribution was never the moat

The instinct in a lot of front offices is to treat this as a control problem — tighten the media clauses, define the windows more narrowly, restrict what a player can publish and when. That instinct will feel prudent and will lose.

It will lose because the thing being protected is not the thing that has value. A media-rights deal is a lease on attention for a fixed period. It is renewable only for as long as the underlying attention keeps showing up, and attention is migrating toward people rather than properties. A restrictive clause does not stop that migration; it just guarantees that when the athlete's audience compounds, none of that compounding happens inside the league's ecosystem.

There is a harder version of the point. A league that restricts athlete media is not preventing a competitor from forming. It is subsidising one — paying the salary of the person who is building it, and then declining to participate.

The question the balance sheet cannot answer

Leagues are extremely good at valuing media rights because media rights are legible. There is a term, a fee, a market comparison, an auction.

The fan relationship is not legible in the same way, which is why it tends not to appear on anyone's balance sheet, and why it is quietly being given away. Ask a simple question about your own organisation: when a fan watches a highlight, follows a player, buys a jersey and argues about a call, who holds the record of that person? In most cases the honest answer is a platform you do not own, under terms you did not write, reachable only by paying that platform again to speak to the audience you generated.

That is not a media-rights problem. It is closer to a customer-data problem, and it has been solved badly in every other industry that hit it first — retail losing the customer to marketplaces, hospitality losing the guest to aggregators, music losing the listener to streaming services. In each case the incumbent kept the revenue line and lost the relationship, and in each case it took about a decade to understand that these were the same thing.

What the creator economy actually offers a league

Here is where our own position is obvious, so we will state it plainly rather than pretend to neutrality. DeHub is a decentralised, open-source social network where a post is minted on-chain to the poster's wallet at the moment of publication, the ad revenue share is published rather than inferred, and subscriptions are tradable assets that pay the original creator a royalty when resold.

Applied to sport, three things follow that are not available on a conventional platform.

Ownership is provable, so it can be shared. If a highlight, a training clip or a post-match reaction is minted to a wallet, then the question of who owns it has an answer that does not depend on either party's goodwill. Athlete-owned, club-owned, jointly-owned — all of these become configurable rather than contested, because ownership is recorded rather than asserted in a clause.

The relationship is portable, which cuts both ways. An audience that belongs to the athlete can leave with the athlete. It can also be brought into a league ecosystem rather than built entirely outside it. The strategic move is not to prevent portability — you cannot — but to be the environment worth staying in.

The monetisation is per-piece. Free, pay-per-view, or token-gated, decided upload by upload. A league does not have to choose between "everything behind the rights deal" and "everything free for reach". Access tiers become an editorial decision rather than a contractual one.

The clause worth writing instead

The reflex clause says: the athlete shall not distribute competing content.

The clause worth writing says something closer to: the athlete's channel is an asset of this relationship, we will help capitalise it, and here is how the value is split.

The first treats the athlete's audience as leakage. The second treats it as inventory the league did not previously have — inventory that keeps producing after the whistle, through the off-season, and, crucially, after the player retires, at which point a conventional rights model has nothing left to sell.

That last point deserves emphasis, because it is the one the current model handles worst. A league's relationship with a fan is mediated almost entirely through active players. When a player leaves, the fan's attachment does not neatly transfer to the badge; a meaningful share of it follows the person. Under the current arrangement, that share leaves the ecosystem permanently. Under a shared-ownership arrangement, it does not have to.

What we are not claiming

We are not claiming that decentralised platforms are about to replace broadcast rights, that fans will move en masse next season, or that any of this is frictionless. It is not. Wallets, on-chain records and token-denominated payouts are unfamiliar to most sports audiences, and unfamiliarity is a real cost. Rights deals will remain the largest line in league revenue for a long time.

The claim is narrower and, we think, harder to argue with: the fan relationship is an asset, it is currently held by third parties, it is compounding fastest in the hands of individual athletes, and no existing rights structure captures any of it.

Leagues understood in the 1980s that owning the broadcast was worth more than owning the stadium. The equivalent realisation this decade is that owning the relationship is worth more than owning the broadcast.

The athletes have already worked this out. That is what the podcast is.

Frequently asked questions

Are athletes really media brands, or is this an overstatement about a handful of stars?

At the top it is unambiguous — athlete-hosted shows draw audiences in the millions and seven-figure sponsorships. Below that tier the effect is smaller but the direction is the same, and it is the direction that matters for a rights negotiation with a ten-year horizon.

Does this mean leagues should stop selling media rights?

No. It means media rights are a lease on attention with a fixed term, and a business whose only asset is a renewable lease is more fragile than its revenue line suggests. The argument is for adding an owned relationship alongside the rights business, not replacing it.

Why would a league want athlete content on a platform it does not control?

It would not — which is the point. The alternative currently on offer is athlete content on a platform nobody in the sport controls, where the terms, the ranking and the rate are all set elsewhere. A platform where ownership is recorded on-chain and the revenue share is published is a different proposition to one where all three are discretionary.

What is the realistic first step for a league or club?

Treat the athlete's channel as an asset in the next contract rather than a risk in the current one, and run one properly resourced pilot with a small group of players — owned, measured, and with the split written down. The finding you are looking for is how much of the fan relationship you can hold directly, not how much content you can produce.
